text: Rating: 4.0/5.0 | Date: 11 20, 2013 | Helpful votes: 0 Heading: Lightweight, easy to load, easy to use, long-term use may be an issue The staple gun is one of those things that we use once or twice a year - especially during haunted house season. The handle is small and made of a plastic material that is smooth - no rough edges on ours which can sometimes happen on machined plastic. It is advertised as fitting small to medium hands, and that it does.Depressing the handle is easy to do, but this is where it differs from other (better) staple guns. On this device you're depressing the handle away from the side that does the actual stapling. This means the weight you're putting on it is at the back and you've got to push forward to hold it against the wood (or whatever you're stapling into).

metadata.product: Arrow Fastener T50X TacMate Stapler

text: This means the weight you're putting on it is at the back and you've got to push forward to hold it against the wood (or whatever you're stapling into). We've had MUCH better success with staple guns where the handle is reversed and you're putting pressure directly into the side that sends the staple downward.Although that might seem counter-intuitive, if you're doing a LOT of staple gunning you're going to notice a difference in how your wrist feels and the level of fatigue you experience. And that's also where the long-term use may become an issue with this staple gun. After a round of stapling it could really be felt in the wrist and arm - due to the "pushing forward" required to hold it against the wood.And so, for light jobs where you aren't spending several hours stapling things down this device works just fine and gets a solid 4 stars. For jobs that require consistent and long-term stapling I'm apt to grab my "reversed" staple gun and use that one, because it works better for my wrist and where the pressure has to be applied.

metadata.product: Arrow Fastener TT21 TruTac Stapler

text: Rating: 3.0/5.0 | Date: 12 4, 2013 | Helpful votes: 0 Heading: Comfortable, simple to use *light* duty stapler The grippy materials help keep your hand from slipping, and the action is triggered by the palm-rest in the opposite way I'm used to with staplers - it hinges at the rear of the stapler, unlike most I've seen where the hinge it at the front. I found it fairly easy to compress the handle enough to staple. These types of staplers alway require a bit extra energy than you might expect coming from a desktop stapler, but this one's not bad.Loading is also easy. Turn the stapler over and pull at the black triangular piece at the back of the base and it slides out. Drop staples into the cavity and close the sliding part. Done.I tested the staples on a small oak board and the staples were consistently embedded about 1/8", leaving a bit more than 1/16" of the staple exposed. This may or may not be the case with lighter woods - this is what I had on hand.

metadata.product: Arrow Fastener TT21 TruTac Stapler

text: This may or may not be the case with lighter woods - this is what I had on hand. It simple doesn't have the power to drive the staple all the way into this wood, so it will need to be for light-duty only (and may prove perfect for hanging Christmas lights because it leaves some of the staple exposed.)The included box of staples is handy. Unless you're stapling a lot, this should last quite a while.Packaging is pretty terrible, for those who worry about such things. It's packed in a plastic blister case, with most of the stapler exposed to allow for testing it out. The stapler is held in by a couple of heat-sealed portions of the blister case and prove a bit difficult to cut around to free the stapler. There's also a small instruction sheet included that really isn't needed once you figure out how to open the staple drawer.

metadata.product: Arrow Fastener TT21 TruTac Stapler

text: Rating: 4.0/5.0 | Date: 11 25, 2013 | Helpful votes: 0 Heading: Handy to have around With the smaller, thinner staples, this little staple gun is perfect for crafts around the home. Perfect for attaching fabric to wood, posters to walls and a myriad of other things where you don't want to use a traditional staple gun or a hammer and nails.This is not the type of stapler you would use for doing heavier work, so it belongs inside and not outside, say in a wood shop. It also operates a bit differently than the traditional staple gun - sort of backwards for a lack of a better description.But if you do a lot of small crafts - you'll soon come to love this little stapler. It's handy and easy on the hands too, if you're needing it for a large number of staples in a piece (I'm thinking something like a plywood backed wreath).

metadata.product: Arrow Fastener TT21 TruTac Stapler

text: Rating: 3.0/5.0 | Date: 11 25, 2013 | Helpful votes: 0 Heading: If you have weak hands read this review! I would have given this 5 stars IF it had been designed in the traditional manner with the arm that you press being opened at the back so I could use the base of my hand verses the top finger area. While it does a nice job and can take 3 diff size staples, it is not only awkward to use but I have weak hands (*I have had cysts drained repeatedly, and a bit of carpel tunnel and osteoporosis, :-( sigh...) and I actually have to use this facing backwards so I can press it utilizing my body weight on my palm area, like I would normally do with a regular stapler. It is sturdy and well built and if you have good strong hands I'm sure you could adapt to this new design, however the old design seems more functional and less tiresome for heavy use or when needing more than a few staples even if you have strong hands. Definitely "crafting grade" not for heavy duty applications. Works very well.

metadata.product: Arrow Fastener TT21 TruTac Stapler

text: Rating: 4.0/5.0 | Date: 11 24, 2013 | Helpful votes: 0 Heading: Wonderful for people like me with poor hand strength I've been using theArrow Co 5700 PowerShot Heavy Duty Staple Gunfor years and I like it so much, I've given one to each of my adult children. The unique body design is so much easier on my hands than traditional style staplers.This new light duty version by Arrow features the same unique design, but is much smaller and lighter in weight. The body is made of a sturdy plastic and the whole thing weighs under a quarter of a pound. It was so lightweight that I really didn't believe the packaging which said it is perfect for small upholstery projects like covering a chair seat. However, I covered 10 chair seats and this stapler had no problem shooting the included 5/16" staples into the wooden seat base. It also works great for cork boards and, using 3/8" staples (not included), it works just fine on drywall.The plastic clamshell that it's packaged in is a pain to open so be warned. Also, be careful not to discard the folded paper instruction sheet because you will need it. It also comes with a box of 1000 5/16" staples.

metadata.product: Arrow Fastener TT21 TruTac Stapler

text: Also, be careful not to discard the folded paper instruction sheet because you will need it. It also comes with a box of 1000 5/16" staples. (You can also use 1/4" and 3/8" staples in this stapler, but they are light duty, thin wire staples so be careful to purchase the correct ones.)The first time you load staples into this stapler, refer to the instructions. It's not like any standard stapler. You turn the stapler over and load the staples from the bottom. You also need to take note of which end the staples come out of. It's not the end you'd think at first glance. However, once you figure it out, this stapler works great. HINT: Press the stapler itself down firmly on the item you are stapling and then squeeze the handle. It takes very little pressure to fire a staple - something I really appreciate when covering 10 chair seats!I think this is a wonderful stapler for light duty projects and craft projects - especially for women or people with arthritis or diminished hand strength. I also recommend its big brother, the PowerShot Heavy Duty Stapler, for heavier use and applications.

metadata.product: Arrow Fastener TT21 TruTac Stapler

Loading staples is a snap (loads like every other stapler out there).Overall I was quite pleased with this stapler and will use it on future projects.

metadata.product: Arrow Fastener TT21 TruTac Stapler

text: Rating: 4.0/5.0 | Date: 11 21, 2013 | Helpful votes: 0 Heading: Light duty stapling only, but comfortable to use. This stapler works pretty good for it's intended purpose but don't expect it to be going into harder words or plywood. text: Rating: 5.0/5.0 | Date: 07 5, 2010 | Helpful votes: 211 Heading: Black & Decker is back! Let me say for starters that I haven't been a big Black/Decker fan for a long time(Black and Decker quit making tough power tools around 1990-1991).If I wanted a power drill currently....I'd buy a expensive/sturdy drill.Secondly,I've used Dremel 395 models for a long time,yes I've found them to be expensive but they do the job.So what could be better than a Dremel tool?A Black & Decker RTX-these are twice the motor power of a Dremel Tool,very well designed and comfortable to use(has a very nice rubber grip for extensive handling options during use),has a universal collet to except a massive range of dremel and aftermarket accessories(including a threaded section for the Flex Shaft),and a cool Flip Lock system to making changing bits a one-handed operation.Did I mention the RTX is half the price of a Dremel Tool.This tool is huge competition against Dremel,and my hopes for the RTX model is that it will become a main staple by Black/Decker and more advanced models will be released years down the road.Get a B&D RTX and save yourself some money :)

metadata.product: Black & Decker RTX-B 3-Speed RTX Rotary Tool Kit

text: Rating: 5.0/5.0 | Date: 10 24, 2010 | Helpful votes: 42 Heading: Wow...Great alternative to Dremels I still have and use my Dremel #245 and my Dremel cordless MiniMite 750, but after reading the other reviews on this black and decker I gave it a try and bought one. My Dremel 245 gets burning hot fast. Wow what a great alternative to Dremel models. My Dremel #245 would heat up tremendously after a short period of use. (Yes I checked the bushings on my Dremel 245 and they are still good on this unit). The black and decker with the 3 speeds was powerful and relatively not too noisy as well. It has a good feel to it, sure its only slightly more girth than a Dremel but the weight distribution and the rubberized plastic where you can hold it made it very comfortable in the hand. Black and Decker has a great alternative and it fits many of the Dremel accessories I have. I have yet to encounter one that didn't fit yet. I used it with my Dremel Chain Saw sharpening tool and it fits and screws on perfectly. Note the amazon description says storage case, its not a carrying case that comes with your Black and Decker, its a draw string black plastic pouch bag.

metadata.product: Black & Decker RTX-B 3-Speed RTX Rotary Tool Kit

text: Note the amazon description says storage case, its not a carrying case that comes with your Black and Decker, its a draw string black plastic pouch bag. The tool sort of fits in that bag. I guess to keep the cost down they opted to give you a pouch bag instead of a hard plastic carrying case, No matter. The tool itself is excellent. It has a 3 speed dial labeled L (12,000), M (24,000) , H (30,000) . Who needs more than that? I'm very happy with it. If you always had a dremel like me, give this black and decker a try and you will be surprised at the high quality of this rotary tool.Update (Jan 2013) Get the dremel keyless chuck. It fits and works on this Black and Decker Tool and you will never have to bother with the collet and collet wrench again. Really. Once you do that, you will never go back to using collets on this black and decker rotary tool.

metadata.product: Black & Decker RTX-B 3-Speed RTX Rotary Tool Kit

text: Rating: 5.0/5.0 | Date: 07 19, 2011 | Helpful votes: 9 Heading: This is a seriously good tool! I used to buy Dremel tools fairly frequently. They were very useful, but they didn't hold up well. To be fair, they were fairly heavily abused. But they would break pretty easily, and I got tired of fixing them and replacing them... The brushes would get hot and melt the brush holders, the electronics for the variable speed would fail, etc, etc, etc. I would spend $80 a couple times a year buying Dremel tools.I bought this as a replacement for the Dremel about 8 years ago, and I use the heck out of it... metadata.product: Black & Decker RTX-B 3-Speed RTX Rotary Tool Kit

text: Rating: 5.0/5.0 | Date: 12 20, 2011 | Helpful votes: 2 Heading: Restored my faith in Black and Decker products It did in fact restore my faith in Black and Decker products! I was between this one and a dremel and I am very happy I bought this one! It takes all the dremel accessories out there, comes with a complete set of collets for all sizes of accessories and mounts very positively to generic drill presses (have a Milescraft 1097). Changing bits is easy as a small lever right next to the on/off switch locks the spindle to allow easy accessory removal and installation. The most impressive though is its power. Even at the lowest speed it can go through 1mm aluminum sheet or fiberglass reinforced epoxy (Printed Circuit Board material) like a hot knife through butter. I only needed the medium speed setting when I was drilling through 1mm sheet steel. Still haven't used the high speed setting for drilling only for cutting half an inch thick steel bolts with a carborundum cutting wheel which it did in less that 10 seconds! Mounted on a drill press it can easily drill 0.6 -0.7mm holes on PCB with absolute precision and almost noiseless!

text: Rating: 5.0/5.0 | Date: 11 21, 2011 | Helpful votes: 2 Heading: Very nice tool This is a very nice tool that can do almost anything. It is also just as good as a Dremel because I once had one of those. For 1/4 the price as well it's a steal. It also has a nice lock/unlock function that the dremel didn't for safety when changing bits. I have to remember to use that though when I am using the flex shaft. But this tool does a very nice job at finishing off wood. Hollowing out wood takes some time, but I think I need thicker cutters for that than the ones I have. The stuff that comes in this kit is a carrying pouch, the tool, 2 coarse sandpaper drums, 3 finer sandpaper drums, and the handy wrench tool. It has 3 speeds, low, medium, and high. text: Rating: 5.0/5.0 | Date: 01 5, 2014 | Helpful votes: 1 Heading: B&D delivers a very functional, powerful, and economical rotary tool… My battery poweredDremel 7300did a good job, except that the battery always seemed to be dead, whenever I wanted to use the tool. This provided the motivation for buying an AC powered rotary tool. Both Black and Decker and Dremel were under consideration, but when the B&D; RTX-B dropped down to $23, I made my choice, as it was half the price of theDremel 200 kit.An AC powered motor can deliver more power and torque, which typically means, more dramatic results. The RTX-B motor has three speeds, 12,000 RPM, 24,000 RPM, and 30,000 RPM. I generally use the lowest speed for better control, but it's great to have a lot more power available if it is needed. The battery powered Dremel 7300 has a top speed of 13,000 RPM, and delivers much less torque.The RTX-B has an ergonomic design, with a rubberized area near the front, that provides a nice grip. The tool incorporates a pretty well designed flip lock safety mechanism to lock the shaft.

metadata.product: Black & Decker RTX-B 3-Speed RTX Rotary Tool Kit

text: The tool incorporates a pretty well designed flip lock safety mechanism to lock the shaft. Replacing fittings and accessories isn't as easy as the Dremel, but at least the chuck accepts all my old Dremel accessories, and does a superior job with them. This is fortunate, as when it comes to accessories, Dremel's product line is far superior, leaving B&D; in the dust.Some may not think it necessary, but with a rotary tool capable of high speeds, wearing safety glasses is a must. A carrying bag that isn't well suited to the tool is included, along with some screwdriver bits.While Dremel accessories are the best, they don't necessarily have to be attached to a Dremel brand rotary tool. Although the price has risen to close to $30, the B&D;'s RTX-B is a solid performer, which still remains less expensive than the Dremel 200 kit, and I don't have any second thoughts about buying one.

text: Rating: 5.0/5.0 | Date: 02 10, 2009 | Helpful votes: 9 Heading: The Magnum Holeshooter of Jigsaws I was told you couldn't go wrong. That was an understatement.Running down the list:* Yes, very tight scroll cuts. No, you can't twist the blade violently to make a 90 degree cut. That's just common sense physics and not what people mean by "square" cuts. It does plunge cut quite nicely with the the right blade though. If the blade is wandering on you, press the big shiny red button and read the manual fer cryin' out loud. I didn't even have one and I figured out what you needed to lock down the precision control mechanism.* It couldn't be easier or more obvious how to change blades if a little gnome hopped out of a hole in the gearbox and did it for you. Seriously.* It's the right weight in my opinion which aids in control and stability but most people would get tired fast using it on walls or ceilings.

metadata.product: Bosch 1590EVSK 6.4 Amp Top Handle Jigsaw

text: Seriously.* It's the right weight in my opinion which aids in control and stability but most people would get tired fast using it on walls or ceilings. Get a JS5 or dig deep for the festool if you need a lighter saw for this purpose or just get a sawzall if you don't need a clean cut.* As far as bevel control, straight and 45 degree bevel cuts are really easy to set up because there are indentations you can slide the foot back on for these settings. You can set up any angle in between but it probably takes a little trial and error to get precision out of this. The surfaces that come into contact are rough (probably to hold tighter when locked) so you basically have to loosen it enough for them to not be in contact which is kind of wobbly and clumsy. It's a minor but standout gripe in an otherwise near-perfectly engineered tool and the friction that makes a smooth adjustment tricky is probably also part of what keeps the setting rock solid when you lock it down. That is IF you know there is a lever and a dial for locking/unlocking and tightening/loosening.

metadata.product: Bosch 1590EVSK 6.4 Amp Top Handle Jigsaw

text: That is IF you know there is a lever and a dial for locking/unlocking and tightening/loosening. That's another RTFM issue some people are missing, I suspect.* I have no idea why you would need variable speed trigger control on it. It's too smooth of an operator to need a soft start and I would anticipate no trouble continuing an aborted cut. It's not going to jerk around on you when you start it up again. I think Bosch's engineers were reasonable in assuming you'd be cutting one type of material at a time with it so why would you need to adjust speed as you go?* Blower works great. The dust collection attachment looks like it will work well but I haven't had a chance to purchase/try it yet.* As for longevity/toughness: I got mine fairly heavily used. The beat-up case and marks and wood glue gunked up on the saw suggest quite a bit of use from an on-site contractor who wasn't a very light touch. Also some abuse/misuse: there are scratch marks on the foot-loosening dial that suggest he didn't RTFM either and the blade in it is pretty seriously scorched for the edge its teeth are still holding.

metadata.product: Bosch 1590EVSK 6.4 Amp Top Handle Jigsaw

text: In spite of all this, I can't imagine the saw ever worked better than it does now.* Controls: 3 orbital settings or no orbital on one switch. Blower toggle. Precision guide toggle. Foot locking lever for locking in a new bevel setting. Foot loosening/tightening dial for setting the bevel before locking the foot again. Speed control in the back where it could be a touch awkward to reach for during use but I don't see why you would need to. Nonvariable speed trigger with a rightie/leftie-friendly trigger lock that would come in handy if you want to mount it upside down to use like a scroll saw table.* Cuts that you won't have to sand if you use the right blades. You can credit the dual-edge-cutting miracle blades Bosch makes for this (I was using one of the older ones) but the negligible vibration and control the saw gives you can't hurt.I can't tell you this is the best jigsaw, not having tried its immediate competitors but I can certainly say it's a 5-star experience and much better than not going wrong. Definitely worth spending the extra bucks over some black & decker POS and the JS5 is probably better than any disposable consumer grade model if the cost is an issue for you.

Two metal jaws in constant contact with a metal blade moving at 3000 spm, with no lubrication or rollers. I initially thought the saw had a bad motor bearing as it consistently squeaked to a stop. text: Rating: 3.0/5.0 | Date: 05 26, 2005 | Helpful votes: 110 Heading: 2 years later ....... I've had this router package for about two years now & use it on average 2 or 3 times a week. At first I thought it was the greatest thing since sliced bread. Now that the honeymoon is over I've come to the conclusion that it's a decent design with a few minor annoyances & a couple of major faults. Some nice idea's but the execution leaves a lot to be desired.1. I like the handles on the plunge base, good ergonomics, good control. I don't like the wooden handles on the fixed base. Poor fit & finish. They regularly come loose & need to be retightened. Lockwashers don't help. I don't use locktite because I remove the handles for some of the jigs & baseplates I use.2. I love the 8 position turret on the plunge base. This should be an industry standard.3. The Bosch plunger is a normally locked type. I like the plunge lever to be normally unlocked like Hitachi & DeWalt it makes it much easier to set depth of cut.4. Changing bases. When the router is cold it's a wrestling match to remove the base. It gets better as it warms up & then becomes too loose on the plunge base.

metadata.product: Bosch 1617EVSPK 12 Amp 2-1/4-Horsepower Plunge and Fixed Base Variable Speed Router Kit with 1/4-Inch and 1/2-Inch Collets

text: Changing bases. When the router is cold it's a wrestling match to remove the base. It gets better as it warms up & then becomes too loose on the plunge base. I've tried adjusting the screw on the latch & haven't been able to hit the magic spot yet.5. The fine adjustment on the fixed base. This is undoubtably related to the previous issue. It's too tight when it's cold & then gets easier as it warms up. The adjustment knob helps quite a bit. But then you can't turn it over on it's head to change bits unless you balance it on the edge of the table. Kind of a pain. Also the knob has to be removed to remove the motor. Too many steps, too many parts. I prefer the simple continuous adjustments that DeWalt & Milwaukee use.6. Template guides. These are OK but again too many parts, levers & steps leave too much room for error. I made baseplates that accept PC type guides. Much better.7. The edge guide is a nice unit.8. text: Rating: 3.0/5.0 | Date: 06 25, 2010 | Helpful votes: 10 Heading: good motor, poor bases I've logged several hundred hours with this router, using both bases. I like the motor, with it's variable speed and soft start, and have had no issues with it bogging down or bad switches. Then again, I've only used it on soft woods like fir and redwood, and only rarely used bits over 1.5". My main issues are with the bases. When it was new, it was easy to swap the motor from one to the other, but over time the grooves which hold the motor in place in the bases put deep scratches in the motor sides (the edges of the grooves are pretty sharp), and due to the increased friction, it has become a serious headache switching back and forth.I have the fixed base mounted in a router table, and do freehand work with the plunge base. I've discovered that the fixed base is obviously not intended to be permanently mounted inverted in a table. When inverted, the only thing which holds the shaft of the fine adjustment screw in place is a tiny little snap ring.

metadata.product: Bosch 1617EVSPK 12 Amp 2-1/4-Horsepower Plunge and Fixed Base Variable Speed Router Kit with 1/4-Inch and 1/2-Inch Collets

text: When inverted, the only thing which holds the shaft of the fine adjustment screw in place is a tiny little snap ring. This means that when the release lever is open, the entire weight of the router is supported by a thin piece of metal, and when you raise and lower the router with the screw, a lot of force is placed on this thin ring. Over time, the snap ring will deform, and eventually fly off or break, making height adjustment impossible. Setting the bit height exactly is also an issue, as the bit will pivot slightly when the lever is tightened, changing the height by as much as 1/32".Also, be aware that if you intend to use the motor in a table with a router lift, the motor is not the same diameter as the standard porter cable that most router lifts are designed to fit. Adaptors are available, but then that's one more hassle.

metadata.product: Bosch 4100-09 10-Inch Worksite Table Saw with Gravity-Rise Stand

text: I'll replace it when it's not making glue-ready cuts, but for now, it's all good.The only, tiny weakness here? If you use the miter gauge for anything requiring accuracy, you're going to need to replace it as soon as you can afford to. It wobbles left and right in the slot, which means that two cuts with the miter set to 45 degrees might add up to 85 or 95 degrees, but rarely average out to a perfect 90. I built a miter sled to fix the problem; $10 of MDF, scrap maple for runners, and a few screws. A buddy of mine swears by the Incra miters, but those are $100+.The zero-clearance insert (also sold on Amazon) isn't bad, but if you press downward too much with a piece of wood, the insert bends down, and the cut will be at a slight angle. Not a sturdy piece of plastic. The fix is pretty simple, but time consuming again; take a piece of hardwood and build the inserts yourself.

The ripping fence also shows cost-cutting - rather than gear controlled, you clamp and un-clamp it and slide it to position it. text: Rating: 5.0/5.0 | Date: 07 18, 2011 | Helpful votes: 7 Heading: Great DIYer's saw; portable yet good for small shops... I'm late to the game with this saw review -- I've owned mine for over two years and used it extensively for all the framing work of a full-scale home foundation, remodel and basement build-out. Yes, it's portable, but although mine is "stationary" in my house, it's moved from room to room depending on where the work is and to make way for continuing work.Since this saw has been reviewed to death, here's my quick list of pros and cons:+ This saw is very portable. It folds quickly, rolls on pneumatic tires, so is perfectly at home on a job site.+ Soft start means no blowing of GFCI breakers.+ Fence is extremely accurate. I usually verify with a tape to ensure cut is square from front to back of fence, but more often than not this step is unnecessary.+ Very good dust collection. A Craftsman shop vac is all I have connected to the dust port and I'm fairly happy with this saw's ability NOT to kick wood dust back up into the air.- 10" blade means this saw is unable to rip 4x and 6x lumber.

metadata.product: Bosch 4100-09 10-Inch Worksite Table Saw with Gravity-Rise Stand

text: Very, very often I find it is necessary to perform two cuts to rip lumber that's destined for furring out walls.I'm totally happy with this unit and glad I spend the extra money on it (and its stand) versus a unit from Ridgid or Craftsman. I'm OK with the complicated blade guard design, which mostly stays out of my way (or completely detached). Height and angle adjustments are quick, easy, and accurate enough for framing and rough-in construction. I had anticipated selling this unit after completion of my remodel, but am not thinking that because it stores compactly, it would be a good saw to keep stored away that would easily roll out into an open area of the garage or front yard to perform those random cutting tasks we all have.

text: Rating: 5.0/5.0 | Date: 01 26, 2010 | Helpful votes: 7 Heading: Need portable accuracy? This is it. I wanted something portable yet accurate. I researched quite a few table saws online and read all of the consumer reviews before deciding on the Bosch. The first saw I got home and assembled was DOA. The power switch was kapoot. So I returned the saw and got a replacement - perfect.First of all, I especially like the safety features. The riving knife works great, and the anti-kickback pawls can save your life. The rip fence is dead-on accurate. I'm still learning more about the rip fence with the side extended, but think I've figured this out. I can now confidently set the fence per the markings and get a reliable cut. The miter gauge works really well and feels very sturdy.The gravity lift stand is pure genius and allows me to stow the saw in a corner when it's not needed. Setup takes less than 30 seconds including plugging this baby into a 120 Vac outlet. The soft-start motor is a thoughtful design feature too. The saw's motor runs loudly enough to let you know it means business.

metadata.product: Bosch 4100-09 10-Inch Worksite Table Saw with Gravity-Rise Stand

text: The soft-start motor is a thoughtful design feature too. The saw's motor runs loudly enough to let you know it means business. I have a friend who nearly sawed his hand in two while vacuuming his shop and he didn't notice that his saw got turned on, so the loud motor isn't really detrimental to me.On the rear of the saw is the electrical cord storage area, a very handy push stick (safety first!) and the saw dust exhaust port. This port connects directly to my shop vac and I'd say that better than 90% of the dust is captured into the vacuum. If you don't connect a dust collector, this port spews dust a good distance, probably around 8 feet or so.The saw's construction put metal where it is needed, and sturdy plastic where it is not. This makes the saw light enough to be carried around if you choose not to use the lift stand. But this stand is so good, so portable, and so sturdy, you will want to use it.So despite my first disappointment with a defective power switch, my overall satisfaction with this saw is extremely high. After using a small 8" bench table saw for over 25 years, now I feel like I've graduated to the major league and can make saw dust with the best of them.

text: Rating: 3.0/5.0 | Date: 05 28, 2007 | Helpful votes: 221 Heading: Good tool I already own three other "full size" routers so this little router is quite a pleasant surprise to use. It is light weight and very solid; hinge-mortising, edge-triming, and rounding-over are a breeze. I also bought the round subbase so that it can be used with my Porter-Cable templet guide set and it works out quite nicely. So why is only 3-stars? As mentioned by other reviewers, the "Shaft-Locking Button" does not hold and needs to be redesigned. text: Rating: 1.0/5.0 | Date: 10 20, 2012 | Helpful votes: 5 Heading: HUGE disappointment While Hate is not really a word to use on an inanimate object, it comes pretty close to how I feel about this little machine.I'm a professional contractor and rely on my tools to perform. A small router is a great tool to have as it allows you to work in tight spaces. I have purchased MANY Bosch tools in the past and in general have been happy with the brand. The Bosch Colt, however, has failed in so many ways costing me time and money.Shortcomings:Depth Control: The router base is supposed to clamp to the motor securing the depth. The cam device on this router does not adequately secure the motor. (Yes, I have tightened the nut and cam to no avail). As you move the router across the work piece, I can actually feel the motor slide down into the base resulting in a deepening groove. text: Rating: 4.0/5.0 | Date: 05 28, 2012 | Helpful votes: 3 Heading: Use both wrenches I've been on the fence over whether or not this thing was worth the price of entry for a few years now, and all the one star reviews were a big factor in that. When I saw that Stewart Macdonald had begun making guitar repair jigs for it I figured it had to be worth a shot and picked one up to help square up some rough edges that resulted from my using a circular saw as a miter saw with varying degrees of success.I immediately found that none of those one-star complaints had any validity to them whatsoever. There is no play in the base at all when it is locked correctly (and it's pretty difficult to lock it incorrectly to boot). The shaft lock button engaged just as well as the one on my big router, the bit was perfectly perpendicular--as verified by a Starrett square--and I didn't really need a manual to get up and going in minutes. I will say that perfect centering is not something you should expect with the included base.

metadata.product: Bosch PR20EVSK Colt Palm Grip 5.6 Amp 1-Horsepower Fixed-Base Variable-Speed Router with Edge Guide

text: I will say that perfect centering is not something you should expect with the included base. It's more of a quick-and-dirty affair than something you'll ever want to do inlay with, but the fact that it doesn't accept templets should be a pretty big clue there.One problem I did experience was the bit dropping out of the collet. This happened twice and I was getting a mite peeved, but then on the third try I used the second wrench rather than the shaft lock button when tightening and had no further problems. This is generally recommended practice with most routers, so I can't fault the Colt for that. The second wrench *is* in the box these days, so don't let those complaints deter you.Didn't think I'd need the variable speed, but it did scorch pine on 6. Backing it off to 5 helped tremendously. It definitely runs warm, but use some common sense and it shouldn't overheat--deep cuts should always be done incrementally no matter how much horsepower you've got to work with.I wouldn't dream of making it my only router, but it beats the pants off of any Dremel I've ever used.

text: Rating: 5.0/5.0 | Date: 01 6, 2010 | Helpful votes: 5 Heading: Effective dust collection for a decent price After using this dust bag for months now, I am pleasantly surprised at how much dust the bag actually collects. Of course not, and it would be unreasonable to expect that it would. I am puzzled at some reviews that knock the product for not comparing favorably to a true dust collection system. I use the bag on a Bosch 4100-09 unit and use both the stock and zero clearance inserts. Contrary to some reviewers, I have not found the bag to significantly restrict output airflow.At home I use a dust collection system, but on the road this bag works well and saves cleanup time at the end of the job. I think if you keep your expectations reasonable, you will be satisfied with this dust bag.

text: Rating: 1.0/5.0 | Date: 02 2, 2012 | Helpful votes: 14 Heading: battery contacts are the Achilles heel of this tool I've owned four of these saws, and so far, the copper battery contacts have distorted and failed on three of them. I'm leery of using the fourth saw, lest the same happen to it. Unfortunately the copper fingers that contact the battery are part of the power controller and trigger mechanism; you can't buy the replacement battery contacts separately. This power controller part is used on over a dozen Dewalt products, most of which draw less current than a recipro saw does. A replacement part will run at least $60 by the time you get it delivered; if you pay for installation, it comes to more than a new bare-tool saw!The saw itself is very powerful, though it vibrates more than a comparable Milwaukee Sawzall. I now use a28 volt Milwaukee Sawzallinstead, which has battery contacts that won't distort under use.I believe the reason I have seen more failure of the battery contacts than other reviewers is that I often changed to a second or third battery while the tool was hot from use. But my feeling is that a recipro saw is made to be pushed hard.

text: Rating: 2.0/5.0 | Date: 09 20, 2010 | Helpful votes: 9 Heading: Not a replacement for a corded model... I have both this saw and the coded Dewalt reciprocating saw. I generally like Dewalt tools but I can't recommend this one. One would expect a difference in power between the corded and cordless model, but there is another very fundamental difference. Let me explain with an example of how I tried to use these saws yesterday. I was replacing a window in my house with glass block which required me to increase the size of the opening in the house by about 1.5". To do this, I decided that I needed to saw (rip) through a layer of dry wall, a 2x4 in the 3.5" dimension, and a 1/2" fiber board. I needed to rip off 3/4 of an inch along each 5' side.I first tried with the cordless model. It would cut through wall, but jumped and rattled so badly that the cut was very very rough and it jumped so much that it destroyed the drywall. I then switched to the corded model. It smoothly and cleanly sliced through the wall. No comparison at all. My net is that if you don't absolutely need a cordless model, go for the corded one and the Dewalt is a good choice there.

text: Rating: 3.0/5.0 | Date: 11 21, 2010 | Helpful votes: 132 Heading: An Average Circular Saw, Satisfactory For Home Owner Use At the current time, cordless saws have noticeably less power than corded tools. The DeWalt DC390 is no exception to this. It will certainly cut 2" thick fir and pine lumber, but you won't get the same rate of production as with a corded saw.This saw has a thick base plate, which I like. Thinner stamped metal base plates on circular saws often get bent after several years of use and the saws never work well after this happens.A routine use of the DeWalt DC390 will be to cut thin stock such as plywood. It's handy to have a cordless tool for this purpose since you often have to extend your reach to make cuts. However, this saw is poorly balanced for such work. With the cut depth set shallow, the battery is raised high and the saw is top heavy. If you put the saw down as you would a normal circular saw, it will tip over. The lower half of the saw guard is made of a slightly flexible plastic. Given this saw is likely to tip off worktables frequently, I think this is better than having a metal guard which might get permanently bent.

metadata.product: DEWALT Bare-Tool DC390B 6-1/2-Inch 18-Volt Cordless Circular Saw

text: Given this saw is likely to tip off worktables frequently, I think this is better than having a metal guard which might get permanently bent. Plywood is often cut using a guide such as a bar of metal clamped to the work. It is difficult to cut with the DeWalt DC390 while keeping it snug to a guide because, in addition to the trigger, the saw has a safety that must be pressed with your thumb. It prevents you from wrapping your thumb around the handle, so you don't have a normal grip. (The DC390 also suffers from a weakness of all direct drive circular saws in that the motor leaves little clearance under it and tends to bump into any clamps that you use to hold the guide. It seems to me that manufacturers could do a better job of designing a motor housing that provided more clearance, even if only when the saw is set to do shallow cuts and motor is raised relatively high.)The locking knobs for the bevel and depth of cut are made of hard plastic. I find them comfortable to use.The saw uses a 6 1/2 inch diameter blade with a 5/8 inch arbor hole. The blade included with the saw has 16 teeth and is for rough carpentry.

metadata.product: DEWALT Bare-Tool DC390B 6-1/2-Inch 18-Volt Cordless Circular Saw

text: I find them comfortable to use.The saw uses a 6 1/2 inch diameter blade with a 5/8 inch arbor hole. The blade included with the saw has 16 teeth and is for rough carpentry. (It is easy to find a variety blades that fit this saw in hardware stores. Don't buy a blade with a 10 mm arbor by mistake. The arbor bolt is reversed threaded and must be tightened with a hex key. The key is provided and it can be stored securely by pressing it into slots in the body of the saw.Like many cordless saws, this is a "left handed" saw, which has the blade mounted on the left side of the motor. For a right handed person, the consequences of a "left handed" saw are these: When you cut along a marked line, you will be able to see where the blade is cutting clearly because the motor won't be in the way. However, when you perform the typical operation of holding a board down with your left hand while you cut off the right end of the board, the wider part of the saw's base is resting on the wood that will bend and fall away. The saw also tends to tilt and fall away.

metadata.product: DEWALT Bare-Tool DC390B 6-1/2-Inch 18-Volt Cordless Circular Saw

text: The saw also tends to tilt and fall away. You have to apply attention and force to keep the base of the saw level.This particular product offer ( DC390B, "tool only") does not include a battery for the saw or a charger. The saw's shipping weight is listed as 8 lbs ( about the weight of a plastic gallon jug of water) and, to me, this feels correct for the weight of the tool. Attaching a battery adds weight. At the current time ( Nov. 2010) DeWalt makes both 18 V Nicad batteries and more expensive and lighter 18 V lithium batteries that fit its 18V cordless tools.I rate this saw as three stars out of five to indicate that it is an average cordless saw. It may be a better than average deal depending on your requirements and its current price.

text: Rating: 5.0/5.0 | Date: 05 27, 2010 | Helpful votes: 32 Heading: Compact and powerful Not long ago a friend gave me an extra DeWalt 18 volt drill he'd come into. I'd been using a 12 volt Makita for over a decade, and I was impressed with how much more torque and battery life the DeWalt had. The same friend also had a DeWalt impact driver from the same series, and again, I was impressed how well this handled mechanical tasks usually relegated to a pneumatic impact driver. But even more impressive was how well the DeWalt worked for driving screws.A few years ago, the major cordless tool makers started to come out with impact drivers which they marketed not to mechanics, but to carpenters. While today's 18volt cordless drills do a pretty good job of driving screws, they still start to bog down when driving really long screws into hard or resinous wood. The slow, stall, and eventually overheat. But impact drivers don't do this. They work on a different principle, using a motor-driven hammer to repeatedly strike an anvil that drives the output shaft.

metadata.product: DEWALT Bare-Tool DC825B 1/4-Inch 18-Volt Cordless Impact Driver

text: But impact drivers don't do this. They work on a different principle, using a motor-driven hammer to repeatedly strike an anvil that drives the output shaft. As the load increases, they switch from spinning to a rapid-fire staccato impact mode, in which every impact turns the screw a bit farther, while the motor continues to spin and bring in cooling air.I was very pleased to discover that Amazon had a DeWalt impact driver available in a batteryless and caseless package (for those of us who already have a charger and several batteries) for about $125. I purchased mine for a mix of yard projects- this is a great tool for driving the big screws used to tie landscape timbers together- home projects, and motorcycle/scooter maintenance. And amazingly, it's even lighter and more compact than theDEWALT DC759KA Heavy-Duty 18-Volt Ni-Cad 1/2-Inch Cordless Drill/Driver Kit. I'm giving away my Makita 12v drill/driver to a nephew who likes tools and gadgets, and switching 100% to the DeWalt system.

While the dust collector works pretty well (until it tears, that is), it is small and you have to stop work often to empty it. text: Rating: 5.0/5.0 | Date: 06 22, 2011 | Helpful votes: 28 Heading: One of the best value orbitals I do a load of furniture, and floor refinishing. They all have metal-ball bearing construction, all have direct port bags, and can be found for under $50. Anyone who says they can tell the difference between the 3 amp models by those companies is overselling their expertise, especially those who claim to be the experts.I just have good experience with all tools DeWalt makes. metadata.product: DEWALT D26451K Corded 3 Amp 5-Inch Random Orbit Sander with Cloth Dust Bag

text: The older of the two was very used when I started remodeling with my dad, and since then we have sanded 20 kitchen cabinets; all the seams of individual floorboards of a 1,500ft2 oak floor; two large oak tables, a fur table, and two pine tables; a dozen fur chairs; and a ton of custom trim, railings, and molding; and it still works as good as the new one I just bought. Personally I just use shop fans and blow the dust outdoors and clean up the rest with a shop vac when I'm done. You could hook it directly to a shop vac and use perforated sanding disks. text: Rating: 4.0/5.0 | Date: 07 20, 2013 | Helpful votes: 1 Heading: Hated or Loved - Depends Whom I Ask My first cordless tool set was Dewalt, an expensive set. I've also near dozen Dewalt cordless tools I use for home projects, not job related or heavy daily type use.I've read plenty Review and gather folks either dislike or love for most part with little middle ground, and, most displeased Reviews concern premature brick failure - common factors I find:> Bricks placed onto charging cradle while hot/warm> Bricks only charging for a short period 1 - 4 hours> Bricks taken from cradle and placed immediately into service (brick still warm from charging)> Brick rarely allowed a 'refresh' 24-hour chargeThere're certainly others but these are most common I've found.I've tried to avoid practices listed above (home-use allows such) and all six bricks have negligible degradation. By design, Dewalt's Charger will enter a refresh mode if brick remains on cradle past 8 hours (per manual).

text: Rating: 5.0/5.0 | Date: 06 2, 2013 | Helpful votes: 7 Heading: Sharp, long-lasting, pricing is quirky These Dewalt titanium-coated drills are some of the best I've used. When new, they are nearly as sharp as machine-shop drill bits, and the coating keeps the edge useful for a LOT of drilling. I had one 1/2" pilot-point bit last through more than 50 holes through 1/4" to 1/2" steel plate.However, note that once dull, when you sharpen the bit, the coating goes away and so does the longevity of the edge. After sharpening, these drills are good for only 5-10 holes in steel before they dull up again. Kind of disposable in a way. Also, the pilot point drill bits can't be sharpened in a Drill Doctor or any such machine; they have to be hand-ground. Again, sort of a disposable bit. After mine get dull, I'll sharpen them once and then use them only on wood. Since it costs $14 to replace the 1/2" bit, and $24 to get a whole set - - well, you get the idea.

text: Rating: 1.0/5.0 | Date: 08 21, 2001 | Helpful votes: 130 Heading: Lacking some engineering I read the reviews and had it narrowed down to two jointers; DeWalt and Porter Cable. I decided that the price was right on the DeWalt and figured it would do the job. I tested a few joints with it and noticed that the wood was a little off. I figured that it was user error and continued on with my project. Then I decided to check for sqareness off the adjustable fence. The pointer lined up just past the "0" mark and sure enough it was off. No problem, I thought, since it had an adjustment screw, I could not adjust it to where I needed it to go. I had to file the stop block to get it at "90". This failed to fix the problem with the line up of the wood. I finally measured the cut and found that it was a 32nd higher on the right side of the cut. No matter how I hold the tool to the surface it was off. A visual look at the blade and you can see the blade comes out at an angle. Bottom line, the mechanics of the tool are strong, but the machining of everything else hooked to the motor needs more attention. It is going back tomorrow.

text: Rating: 5.0/5.0 | Date: 06 1, 2000 | Helpful votes: 29 Heading: The Best Plate Joiner I've Seen I bought this plate joiner about a year ago, and it has become a regular part of my woodworking activities. It adjusts easily for doing either straight plunges in a 90-degree edge, or for plunging into a 45-degree mitered edge. This is made possible because the fence adjusts to any angle you would ever need. The blade goes a long way before it dulls -- I used mine for at least six months of regular cutting. The saw has solid adjustments for bisquit sizes (#0, #10, and #20, as well as a kind of "open-ended" size that I don't really understand very well) -- you just have to turn a little knob until it clicks into a clearly marked bisquit-size setting. There are clear, red lines on two places on the plate joiner to align with your bisquit marks, whether you are using the machine horizontally or vertically.

text: Rating: 5.0/5.0 | Date: 07 20, 2009 | Helpful votes: 604 Heading: Good from the box, even better with proper alignment A friend got this six months ago for job-site use. It cut pretty well right from the box. The fence has a rack-and-pinion system that is clever, but not quite perfect. We measured the alignment error and have two fixes. If you want to know about them so you can save some money, read on...Using a TS Aligner, we checked the alignment of the fence. The fence was near-perfect when we backed up to the mark, (going right) but it skewed by as much as four or five-thousandths when we moved the fence to the left. That's because the connecting rod between the two gears flexes and there is some "slop" or "play" in the gears. This is more noticeable when approaching the mark from the right. Sometimes this is referred to "lash-back or back-lash."The easy work-around was to always go past the mark (an inch or so to the left) , then roll the knob back slowly right to the mark and try not to overshoot.

metadata.product: DEWALT DW745 10-Inch Compact Job-Site Table Saw with 20-Inch Max Rip Capacity

text: That works OK, and it is free, but it is a time-wasting nuisance and won't provide the consistent accuracy that good woodworking requires.SO... we replaced the flimsy metal rod that connects the two rack-gears. Instead of the stock rod, we used hardened O1 tool rod, which doesn't twist or flex as easily. The rod costs $12 bucks. We also adjusted the two gears to remove the slop. (loosen set screw, twist gears forward together, then re-tighten) Now we had fair fence parallelism in both directions. Not bad for a twelve-dollar fix... but there is more.After using the saw a while, several of us noticed it made burns marks even with reasonable feed-rates and a new blade. One rainy day, we got out the TS aligner again and checked all the critical alignments. Dewalt uses decent bearings, so the runout was not too bad. But there were a number of other small inaccuracies that added up: arbor run-out, slot-parallelism, fence alignment, blade-alignment etc.It took about an hour of measuring, but the Dial indicator with the TS Aligner helped us get everything literally "dialed-in.

metadata.product: DEWALT DW745 10-Inch Compact Job-Site Table Saw with 20-Inch Max Rip Capacity

text: Now this thing cuts as smoothly and accurately as our five-thousand dollar cabinet saws.The secret is to choose a saw with good bearings and a design that allows adjustments.Dewalt and Bosch contractor saws both qualify.Use a dial indicator with a TS Aligner to accurately measure and adjust EVERYTHING. It takes an hour, but it is worth the effort MANY times over. If you buy a new saw in the box, you have to assemble it anyway, so that isn't much more work. ... You can get professional precision at a fraction of the cost of a cabinet saw. If you don't have a TS aligner, you can use a dial indicator with a magnetic base and a 1-2-3 block set.We cut all kinds of mitered molding and trim. We make custom installations and complex speaker cabinets that require EXACT cuts. After we adjusted this with the TS Aligner, the noise-level was lower and blades stay sharp much longer. That's always a good sign!The beautiful thing about this saw is that we can take it to a site, make measurements on a story-pole and cut exactly to the mark, repeatably and reliably. The saw's design allows you to adjust it, assuming you have the right adjustment tools.

text: Rating: 4.0/5.0 | Date: 06 25, 2003 | Helpful votes: 17 Heading: Strong little driver--well made, fantastic value. Dewalt has really hit a home run on this cordless screwdriver. Like other reviewers, I've used my share of other brands cordless screwdrivers. There's no comparison; the others are like toys after you use this Dewalt. The Black and Decker's produce under 30 inch/pounds and only the Makita produces over 30; the Panasonic slightly more (and it's even more money than the Dewalt!). Nobody is offering a driver that has the torque of the Dewalt. This driver can free you from taking a heavier drill to simply screw fasteners and the speed is truly controlable; the big trigger is easily feathered and very ergonomic.Pros: Extremely robust. Has an aluminum housing, high impact plastic handle and the fit and finish are genuinely quality all-the-way. 2 batteries are included; nice touch. metadata.product: DEWALT DW920K-2 1/4-Inch 7.2-Volt Cordless Two-Position Screwdriver Kit

text: Fantastic torque; you will honestly not believe what this screwdriver can set a screw in. I tried some 2 inch deck screws into pressure treated lumber and was amazed. The other manufacturer's drivers aren't even in the same league. Comes with a nice kit box; typical of almost all Dewalt tools.Cons: At least two reviewers mentioned the main shaft being 'wobbly'. When I first turned mine on, I thought I saw the same thing and was somewhat disheartened. But upon closer examination, I found the source of the problem. If you retract the locking collar that secures the bit, it exposes around 1/4 inch of the shaft. When pulled back this way and turned on, you can see it's NOT the shaft that's out of center; it's the collar. The shaft runs true. One prior reviewer stated he took his apart and found that the collar bushing had a burr on it. I'm not taking mine apart, but general examination of it, likely confirms that this is probably the case. Maybe on a Saturday when I have some extra time to burn, I will take mine apart and grind off this burr. It honestly doesn't affect anything, but it is why I'm only rating it 4 stars.

metadata.product: DEWALT DW920K-2 1/4-Inch 7.2-Volt Cordless Two-Position Screwdriver Kit

text: It honestly doesn't affect anything, but it is why I'm only rating it 4 stars. A 'professional' grade tool should be perfect out of the box; just my .02 cents worth. I do feel that some others that may have just quickly looked at the collar alone spinning may have missed that the shaft is true, it simply looks off center because your eyes follow the collar, in it's normal locked state, it covers the shaft and, thus, makes it all appear to run out-of-true.Unbelievable tool for the money, still. text: Rating: 5.0/5.0 | Date: 04 20, 2004 | Helpful votes: 16 Heading: Heavy Duty This unit defines "heavy duty" as far as cordless screwdrivers are concerned. I was able to charge a depleted 7.2 volt battery in an hour. I removed the sliding chuck ring and found the tension spring was not flat ground on the ends and the plastic sleeve below it had a casting bur left causing the wobble(it made the chuck sleeve tilt when released). I flat ground the spring ends and removed the bur and all is ok now. The shaft was not the problem. I suppose that being made in China instead of the USA may have something to do with it. I called DeWalt and the said that to be competitive the do not make this tool here, it would cost too much. He was not too concerned about the wobble because it does not cause the bit to be off center.

text: Rating: 3.0/5.0 | Date: 01 7, 2011 | Helpful votes: 40 Heading: Unique Concept but hardly makes up for not having a laser line After discovering my $210 Dewalt Miter saw did not have a laser line like every other Miter-saw on the market I went shopping. I soon discovered that the add on laser system made for my saw ($80) apparently didn't work well. Was never true and required constant fiddling. The only other option is this "work light" which also casts a shadow line on the wood your cutting. I personally think the engineers were surprised to see the shadow line and decided to advertise it as a feature. The first thing you should know is the shadow appears as you press the saw closer to the board. When the blade is fully up, the shadow is blurred by the teeth on the blade. You can sort of, kinda tell where it is on you project wood with the blade fully up. Push the blade downward and the shadow line becomes sharper. Its not laser line sharp but still clear enough to make a precision cut. (I had a Craftsman with laser and can tell you they can be way off. I had to compensate by placing the blade behind the line. The work light is bright and useful as well.

metadata.product: DEWALT DWS7085 Miter-Saw LED Work Light System

text: (I had a Craftsman with laser and can tell you they can be way off. I had to compensate by placing the blade behind the line. The work light is bright and useful as well. Installation consists of removing the top of the handle and installing the switch into two existing wire connections. You have to pay attention to which side the clip on the plugs are to get them oriented correctly. You then have to maneuver the top piece on while pressing the connectors to one side to get a flush fit. The second piece installs on the blade housing. Pretty much a no brainer.Bottom line: if you have a Dewalt Miter-saw and plan on keeping it you need this work light. It should of been on the saw when you bought it, but thats Dewalt. You will suffer laser envy when your friends break out their Mitre saws...but unfortunately the Dewalt add on laser is a disaster. So welcome to the shadows...(oh,yes you can see it in the daylight too but the saw has to be pretty far down).

text: Rating: 4.0/5.0 | Date: 10 26, 2009 | Helpful votes: 13 Heading: In many respects, superior to a laser! Like the majority of other opinions written here, DeWalt's LED worklight solution is a great alternative to finicky lasers. I've extensively used two laser units, LaserKerf's add-on unit on a DeWalt 708 (quite nice) and Makita's joke of a laser on their LS1016L 10" miter.Anyhow... as has been already pointed out, the LED needs no adjustment and projects a shadow the width of the kerf. My cuts are dead on.Detractors? A few.The shadow isn't crisp and clear until the blade is lowered at least half-way to the workpiece. This is a minor inconvenience because I've taken to casting my lasers (and now shadows) directly onto a tape measure held against the work piece, eliminating the need to pencil-mark the wood. If I had three hands, this wouldn't be an issue. As I only have two, I have to set the tape measure, lower the blade, adjust my piece without jiggling the tape out of place, then remove the tape without jostling the workpiece out of place.Installation is a little cramped.

metadata.product: DEWALT DWS7085 Miter-Saw LED Work Light System

text: The small connectors that others have noted weren't really a problem, and they're actually quite big when they have to sit just so in the tiny compartment on the saw, nested in amongst the various wires. On my DW717, it took a couple of tries of repositioning the connectors and wires to be able to get the LED unit to set flush on the saw.The switch is tiny AND covered with a loose rubber cover, so it's a bit of an inconvenience to turn the LED on and off if using the saw intermittently. It'd be great if it was a pushbutton instead of a rocker switch, and even better if it had a time-out function of some sort after, say, 15 or 30 minutes of inactivity on the saw.Lastly, for some strange reason, this LED causes a bunch of static interference on my radio whenever it's powered on.All-in-all, a great device that removes ALL of the guess work out of my cuts.

metadata.product: DEWALT DWS7085 Miter-Saw LED Work Light System

text: I have used a few laser miters on the job and they are cool looking and good for doing quick inaccurate cuts. Lasers give people the false sense of security (accuracy) because lasers are precise by nature but how it is mounted will determine how accurate your cuts are. Even if you spend the time to line up your laser as perfectly as possible, I've always run into the same issues you have with guns scopes, the more you move it, and bang it around, the less accurate. And I've had issues with the far and near side not being perfectly at a 90 degree angle to the guide rail. These issues aren't a big deal when framing, but don't attempt finishing work without double checking the old fashion way. Another small laser issue, we would always forget to turn it off because it is only noticable when you look at it. I am liking the idea of using the LED light instead of the laser because I always like to drop the blade (not spinning) on my cut line to perfectly line things up. This light will make it so i don't have to squint as much to see where the blade is going to land.

text: Rating: 4.0/5.0 | Date: 11 14, 2011 | Helpful votes: 4 Heading: So much better than a laser Like many others have stated, the DeWalt LED light is much better than a laser for my use. My last mitersaw had a laser and it was a pain to align and hard to see, even inside my wood shop. The light works very well, with only one small caveat, IMHO. The light (or shadow) only gets sharp to align closely to a critical (fine measurement) cut as the blade gets very close to the piece being cut. The closer you get, the sharper the shadow image becomes, so a final small alignment of your piece can only occur at that point, so clamping your piece can be a problem.However, I rarely ever need to clamp the piece I am cutting. I mostly cut 13/16" material (or less) hardwood and am using an 80-tooth blade. I cut slowly and rarely have a need to clamp, so this is not a major issue for me, but may be for others. Bottom line, so far, I like it (especially compared to a laser).

text: Rating: 4.0/5.0 | Date: 07 9, 2011 | Helpful votes: 2 Heading: Great Addition to Dewalt Miter Saws When looking for compound miter saw, I also considered a laser, but I had mixed feelings. The LED light casts a shadow at the blade so you see the entire kerf width as a shadow. It works. You need to get used to the shadow versus the actual cut line, as there can be a bit of a diffference, but it allows you to make fine adjustments of the stock to align for the cut.The LED works best when the blade is close to the stock to be cut. Further away, the shadow is not sharp. It also works best if the blade is turning, so for final alignment of the cut, the saw should be running. Be careful to start the saw away from the stock as the starting torque will pull the saw down into the wood if you are close when you pull the trigger.I like this light.

You CANNOT see the shadow of the blade without a workpiece in place as the shadow will then fall into the slot for the blade! May be obvious, but bears mentioning.2. text: Rating: 5.0/5.0 | Date: 11 19, 2013 | Helpful votes: 1 Heading: Just what I needed! I'd considered the laser cut line marking accessory for my DW718 several times, but the high price and the so-so reviews made me wait until something better came along. This is certainly what I was waiting for. It took only a few minutes to install this work light on my saw, and the added value became evident very quickly. Not only does this cast a very reliable shadow to indicate the blade's position on the wood, but the bright LED light also lights up the work area quite well. The light has it's own switch although it does obtain power through the saw's power connection. It is not activated by the rotation of the blade like many other cut-line accessories are. I've always considered those systems somewhat unsafe as they require positioning the material after the blade is running, which always adds an element of risk.I don't consider myself a woodworking professional, but I do use my saw often for DIY projects and for some furniture making. I think this is an excellent accessory, particularly for the price, and I would highly recommend it to anyone with a compatible saw.

text: Rating: 5.0/5.0 | Date: 07 29, 2013 | Helpful votes: 1 Heading: Awesome gizmo! I am a perfectionist, frequently told I overbuild things, so I was cautious about the claims DeWalt makes for this device. I read the reviews on Amazon and elsewhere, accepting the negative over the positive. Most of the complaints are about low visibility under direct sunlight, which for the most part is true. However, I don't work under direct sun, even when outside with the saw, which is where I tend to use a DeWalt DW717, on which the LED light is mounted. This thing has made my cuts so much more accurate, with the shadow clearly lining up with the cut. I tried the Irwin-branded laser add on to an old Hitachi non-slider, but it just never gave me the precision I was looking for, with my cuts nearly always off. In bright light conditions, the lasers are also too dim to read, so that makes them equal, and I have read about laser adjustment issues on saws with built-in lasers. DeWalt is really on to something here. If you go for a big 12-incher like the DW780, this gizmo comes installed. Just know that it works best in the shade or inside. Definitely recommended.

metadata.product: DEWALT DWS7085 Miter-Saw LED Work Light System

text: Rating: 4.0/5.0 | Date: 05 27, 2013 | Helpful votes: 1 Heading: Better than a laser. This light is not only a work light, but while being positioned over the actual blade, acts as a true cutting alignment mark for your work piece. The over head light casts a shadow of the saw blade right on the wood being cut. This system seems as though it will not go out of alignment as it is securely mounted in O.E.M. mounting positions. There is a separate on/off switch just behind the D-handle that controls the light and mounts on top of the saw blade replacing a cover that resides there. Both items integrate seamlessly into the saw, (mine a DW717 10" saw). The reason I gave a rating of only four stars is because the light switch is a little difficult to install. There is not much room for the wiring in the switch housing. Be careful not to pinch the wires while screwing down the switch cover. The shadow cast from the blade is not real defined until the blade approaches the work piece, unlike lasers that always throw a defined bright colored line on the work piece.

metadata.product: DEWALT DWS7085 Miter-Saw LED Work Light System

text: Rating: 5.0/5.0 | Date: 03 17, 2013 | Helpful votes: 1 Heading: So much better than lasers Sometimes we tend to over complicate things. As is the case with this little gem, lasers while useful & nerdy cool are annoyingly limited for making sighting tasks simple & efficient. Left of blade or right? The LED system is long over due. I'm sure it may have been a happy accident designed to illuminate your workspace. And carpenters are happy because this does emit some light to aid seeing your material & cut lines on the early mornings & late evenings we find ourselves working from time to time. However, the fact that it shines down the blade is what makes this thing long over due. Casting a shadow off the blade gives you a perfectly placed reference for your cuts. Not left nor right like a laser, not requiring adjustments for different blade kerfs but something as simple as a shadow right on your work surface leave a small sliver of daylight between the shadow & your pencil mark & you're in business. Done. Every bit of time you save is money & this thing pays for itself. It's no wonder the later saws come outfitted already.

text: Rating: 5.0/5.0 | Date: 11 4, 2006 | Helpful votes: 436 Heading: An excellent accessory This is an excellent accessory for the already-versatile rotary tool. The trick to its use is to recognize the inherent limitation of all rotary tools.They are high-speed, low-torque tools. The work is done in the same way that a dentist's drill works: Very light pressure lets the bit in effect shave away the material. As the manual says, you need to adjust the tool so the bit is very close to the workpiece, then slowly lower the bit into it.This means you can't use the Dremel drill press the same way you would use a full-size drill press, where you can bear down on the lever and force the bit to dig into the work. If you try to use it that way, you'll get the "slop" that some other reviewers mention.When it's used correctly-- and the manual makes it very clear how to do so-- this is a very good accessory to have.

My setup consists of a Dremel 4000 running at 35k, the keyless chuck, and of course, the workstation. It works perfectly for what I am doing and even heavier drilling with larger bits through wood is possible up to 1/8".The workstation is excellent and I was almost steered away from it by these people leaving negative reviews. There is also the possibility that negative reviewers are using a different dremel model. the 4000 is quite secure when tightened down and though the ABS plastic mount has some flex, it is rigid enough for the work that the Dremel is designed to handle. the people leaving negative reviews probably are the same people trying to cut through billets of steel with the dremel and complaining because it doesn't have enough torque.

text: Rating: 3.0/5.0 | Date: 04 7, 2013 | Helpful votes: 2 Heading: Not quite a serious tool ... but could be Initial impressions on unboxing were of a decent quality product. Materials are nice and the parts go together well. Upon setting it up, it's clear that the vertical position is off (relative to the baseplate) by 1 - 2 degrees, as others have mentioned. In terms of a DIY fix, it might help to extend the curved slot that limits the rotary movement; I have not yet fully investigated. metadata.product: Dremel 220-01 Rotary Tool Work Station

text: I made bushings from sections of a ballpoint pen refill and this improved things considerably. text: (Remember these rotary tools power accessories based on speed, not on torque. High speed low torque often does not deal with too much continuous load very well. Anyone who knows if this is considered OK or who has long term experience using both together please post a comment.A couple of things that you must keep in mind when using this:1) You really do want to hang the tool up above where you're working when you're using this flex thing. I can't say exactly why, but most likely it has to do with keeping the amount of friction low (increased when more of the shaft is curved vs straight) and keeping the shaft from bending at too sharp of an angle. If you have theDremel 220-01 Work Stationdrill press type thing then that comes with an extendable hanger but I can't see any good reason to buy that thing just to get a hanger. In fact almost anyone could come up with something much less expensive and more secure than using the hanger on that. Screw an eye screw into the ceiling and hang it from a rope or run a "clothesline" across your work area and hang it on a couple of "S" hooks, or something.

metadata.product: Dremel 225-01 Flex Shaft Attachment

text: Screw an eye screw into the ceiling and hang it from a rope or run a "clothesline" across your work area and hang it on a couple of "S" hooks, or something. If you don't hang the tool I doubt the shaft is going to shred itself immediately but I'm sure it won't last as long, will be more likely to get damaged by an accidental sharp bend, and won't be able to run at as high of a speed due to the increased friction.2) NOTE! In case you miss the little note in the box, you really do want to run this thing at high speed for a couple of minutes with it hung straight down and no accessory attached. It'll make some disconcerting little ticking sounds at first but those will stop after several seconds. I suspect the point of this is that you want to evenly distribute the grease inside the shaft before running it while bent or otherwise doing any real work. Again, I doubt you'll shred the thing if you don't do this, but at the very least you might have a little trouble with your grinding, etc, for a minute if you try to use it immediately since it's going to distribute grease or otherwise break itself in when first used no matter what.

The destruction of the flex shaft is an exact result of the misuse of the product. If you are an irresponsible idiot who bends it too far or too much at a higher speed, it will burn out. There are simply too many people who don't know what they're doing when it comes to the flex shaft. To ensure the life of your flex shaft:--->DO NOT BEND FAR--->DO NOT MAKE MORE THAN ONE BEND--->DO NOT OPERATE CONTINUOUSLY ON HIGH SPEED--->DO OIL THE FLEX SHAFT EVERY 20-30 HOURS OF USE--->TIP: Hang the Dremel with the flex shaft hanging down straight into you reach.Just remember; the flex shaft is just a piece of wire in a tube. What do you think would happen if you spun a wire 35,000 times a second and tried to bend it allot while doing so?

metadata.product: Dremel 225-01 Flex Shaft Attachment

text: This flex shaft replaced my original "MultiPro" 225 flex shaft, which came in a kit with myDremel 395 MultiPro. The original shaft wasn't the most comfortable to hold due to its narrow cylindrical design, and eventually began to skip when flexed to more than a 90 angle.Rest assured, this 225-1 shaft IS compatible with that era of older generation Dremels.My comments mirror what others have written in the other reviews:+ The flex shaft is an extremely versatile attachment+ It's great for cutting / grinding / drilling in very confined spaces+ It relieves me from having to support the weight of the Dremel tool when in awkward positions, which can become tiring+ The attachment is very easy to attach with a simple threaded connection+ This newer generation of sculpted plastic grip/handle is very comfortable for extended use, unlike the old model of flex shaftAdditionally, I agree with some of the negatives expressed by others:- Changing bits requires locking the shaft and using the mini wrench to release / tighten the collet- It's almost a requirement to find a way to hang the Dremel from a hook, or somehow otherwise support it; laying it on the ground or workbench or hanging it from the flex shaft is not really a good optionWhat drove me to purchase a Dremel in the first place (after years of thinking about it, but putting it off) was the need to drill in a confined ceiling opening to install a new bathroom ceiling fan.

metadata.product: Dremel 225-01 Flex Shaft Attachment

text: And it wasn't actually the Dremel tool itself, but the flex shaft, that cinched the deal. Since then I've used the flex shaft to hold bits for cutting iron pipe in a very confined space, removing paint and polishing an aluminum bike frame, cutting away stripped bolt heads and notching their shanks for removal, and a bunch of other mundane stuff.Seriously, if you have a Dremel already and find yourself doing odd jobs around the house, you'll find a use for the flex shaft. If you don't have a Dremel but have been considering one, don't buy it without the flex shaft included -- it's a must have attachment.

text: Rating: 5.0/5.0 | Date: 11 25, 2013 | Helpful votes: 1 Heading: You'll wonder how you ever worked without it. I've used a non-Dremel foot-pedal-controlled unit with a flex shaft and it was amazing. Rather than holding onto a bulky motor while trying to make precision cuts, you can have a much lighter stylus-like tool. I hang my Dremel by the bail on a hook when using the flex shaft. The attachment generates a bit more noise than the Dremel by itself, and you can feel the heat building up in the spring coil around the grip end of the shaft after a continuous period of use, but the heat on the tool seems much less than holding it by hand and covering the vent ports. Using a high-speed cutter for excessive material removal on oak will still tire out your hand, but much more slowly than holding the Dremel without the attachment. It should be noted the threaded plastic ring next to the chuck is NOT the standard size and will NOT work with attachments such as the 565 multi-purpose cutting kit (router head), the 575 right-angle adapter, and the A679-02 sharpening kit. I have three Dremels on my bench with different heads: a cutting wheel, a sanding drum, and a high-speed cutter.

text: Rating: 3.0/5.0 | Date: 06 18, 2014 | Helpful votes: 0 Heading: Love this This is a lot of fun, and I love using it. Really glad I bought it. A few things though. The pencil shaft is really only a little smaller and maneuverable than just the dremel. Now this is really a testament to how small the dremel actually is, but the stiffness of the flex shaft makes it only a marginal improvement. Also, now that you have it hooked up, you have to find somewhere to put the dremel tool itself, which takes a crucial second hand. You cant really just set it down either because the shaft is not unlimitedly flexible. It is fine, given the mechanical limitations, but it does have limitations in how far it flexes. The picture is a good representation of its degree of flex.Now the big thing, despite being well constructed and lubricated, the rotation through the flex attachment adds a lot of friction. This plays out in several ways, first, its possible on tough materials that the Dremel doesnt have enough torque and gets slowed. It takes a lot less than without it. And the big one, I was using this to cut a piece of plywood, and my dremel got very hot and burned out.
